intro: “Wichtige Begebenheit” (An Important Event) is No. 6 of Schumann’s Kinderszenen, Op. 15. The piano plays accented A major chords and octaves in a marching rhythm.

sections.label: B · Fortissimo in D major
sections.mNote: Long right-hand chords above descending bass octaves.

sections.label: A′ · Opening A major theme again
sections.mNote: Forte again, with the opening dotted rhythm.

cues.title: Opening, bars 1–8
cues.text: The piece is in three beats to the bar, marked forte, with accents over thick chords and octaves in the left hand. In bar 6 the right hand moves into the bass clef as well.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 10, bars 1–8: forte, accents, octave bass and right-hand bass clef in bar 6. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bars 9–16 in D major
cues.text: The music is now fortissimo and in D major. The right hand holds its chords longer while the bass descends in octaves beneath them. The whole eight-bar section is enclosed in repeat signs.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 10, bars 9–16: D-major chords, descending bass octaves and repeat signs; pitches checked against the Mutopia transcription.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Rellstab’s review, 1839
cues.text: Reviewing Kinderszenen in 1839, Ludwig Rellstab took the title to mean music for children to play. A child would need “three hands”, he complained. He added that even then some of it would be difficult.
cues.evidence: Rellstab, Iris im Gebiete der Tonkunst, vol. 10 (1839), quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 11. Translation from the German. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: A major close, then D major
transitions.how: The opening closes in A major. An A major pickup becomes the dominant of D, and the next bar brings D major chords marked fortissimo. The right hand holds a chord while the bass octaves descend D–A–G–F♯.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 10, bars 8–9; chord and bass pitches confirmed in Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900).

transitions.title: From D major back to A major
transitions.to: A′ · Opening A major theme again
transitions.how: The repeated section ends on D major and a rest. The opening A major chord then returns high in the right hand, above rising A–C♯ octaves in the bass. The dynamic drops back to forte, and the dotted rhythm resumes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 10, bars 16–17 and the upbeat between them.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
